subject: Recap + next tests: Redwood vs hyperscaler price/latency for prototype
messages:
From: Mina Haddad <mina_haddad@redwood.ai>

Cc: Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.ai>, Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.ai>
Date: Mon, 28 Jun 2027 15:02:00 -0700
Subject: Recap + next tests: Redwood vs hyperscaler price/latency for prototype

Thanks again for the call earlier, Jordan — good conversation and helpful context on the integration points. Quick recap and proposed next steps so we keep momentum on the prototype economics comparison.

Key notes from our discovery
- Expected steady-state: ~20 concurrent active sessions (UI-driven clinical queries).
- Avg request length: ~800 tokens (post-tokenization, includes prompt + patient context).
- Burst profile: short bursts up to ~1,500 requests/min for ~5 minutes during batch imports.
- Expected cacheable fraction: ~30-40% (templated clinical prompts / reused procedural text).

Redwood hypothesis / differentiators to validate
- Per-1M-token unit cost materially lower with Dedicated + batching + 8-bit quantization vs hyperscaler managed endpoints for this workload shape.
- KV/prefix caching will reduce TPU/GPU active generation by the cache hit rate; we want empirical cache-hit accounting.
- Smart routing (hosted vs dedicated) can keep latency SLOs while shifting lower-cost backends for non-critical workloads.

Proposed tests (what we'd like to run next)
1) 1M-token priced run (synthetic replay of your traffic profile) on Redwood-hosted and Redwood-Dedicated config — capture tokens, p50/p95 latency, GPU utilization, effective batching fill, and cache hits.
2) Matching run on a hyperscaler managed endpoint (you said GCP is easiest) to capture the same metrics and resulting invoice line items.
3) Short burst stress (5–10 min) to validate tail-latency and autoscale behavior.

What we need from you to make the numbers robust
- A one-hour sample trace (or representative CSV) with timestamped requests, token counts per request, and an indicator for repeat/template requests if possible. I attached "sample-metrics-collection.md" with the exact fields we need.
- Confirmation that 800 tokens/request is a fair average, or your corrected number.

Deliverables and timeline
- Redwood to deliver a first-pass unit-econ sheet (per-1M token, per-concurrent-session) and a short writeup of latency/availability tradeoffs: target by EOD next business day after we receive the sample trace. (See attached redwood-price-modeling-v1.xlsx)
- Set a 30-minute follow-up after we produce the initial numbers to walk the spreadsheet and agree on any assumptions to iterate.

Any objections or additions? If that all looks good, can procurement and security loop in any required reviewers so we can include SOC2/IP/APIs artifacts in the next pass?

Thanks,
Mina 
Senior Solutions Engineer | Redwood Inference
mina_haddad@redwood.ai | (415) 555-0147

Subject: Re: Recap + next tests: Redwood vs hyperscaler price/latency for prototype

Nice summary, Mina. I sketched a quick set of cost scenarios using the 800-token baseline and the concurrency/burst numbers you captured. Attached CSV has the line items; brief highlights below so Jordan/procurement have context.

Assumptions
- Tokenization: GPT-style (approx 0.75 words/token) — 800 tokens/request.
- Effective batching: 1) no batching (worst-case / naive), 2) dynamic batching with 100ms window (realistic), 3) heavy batching (500ms window) for background jobs.
- Cache hit scenarios: 0%, 30%, 60%.

Prelim per-1M-token costs (rounded)
- Redwood Hosted (auto-scale, mixed CPU+GPU): $22 / 1M tokens (no dedicated reservation, includes routing overhead)
- Redwood Dedicated (reserved GPUs, optimized kernels, 8-bit quantization): $9 / 1M tokens (at projected utilization for your workload)
- GCP Managed Endpoint (on-demand): $35 / 1M tokens (includes network + managed infra premium)
- AWS Managed Endpoint estimate (similar to GCP): ~$32 / 1M tokens

Notes on what drives gaps
- Batching: moving from no-batching -> 100ms batching reduces per-token cost by ~25-40% depending on request size distribution.
- Cache hits: each 10% cache uplift is roughly 6–8% lower active generation tokens (nonlinear due to tails).
- Reserved utilization: Dedicated benefits only at sustained utilization; at low utilization advantage shrinks.

Action items for me (I'll own these)
- Run a 1M-token simulated replay using your sample trace and produce tuned numbers for the three batching windows + cache assumptions (deliver by Wed EOD).
- Include a sensitivity table for reserved utilization (50%, 70%, 90%) so procurement sees commit vs on-demand math.

Attachment: 1m-token-scenarios.csv

-Ben
Director, Solutions Engineering | Redwood Inference

Thanks both — this is helpful. A few clarifications from our side so the numbers reflect real workload: 

Clarifications
- Avg tokens/request: our sample export shows 720 tokens median, 980 tokens mean (distribution skewed by long documents). Using 800 as a working average is fine.
- Concurrency: steady-state ~20 active sessions. Peak import bursts are short but can hit up to ~25k tokens/sec for 3–6 minutes (that aligns with our batch ingestion jobs).
- Cacheable fraction: roughly 35% (we can annotate repeats in the trace).

Procurement/security asks
- Can you include expected invoice line items for the 1M-token runs (compute, storage, egress if any) so our procurement can map to budget lines?
- Please attach SOC2 and data handling summary for Redwood-hosted and what changes for Dedicated/Private.

Next tests we prefer
1) Redwood-hosted 1M-token replay + latency profiling (we'll provide trace by EOD today)
2) If possible, a short Redwood-Dedicated proof-of-concept (1 day reserved) to measure utilization and batching empirically — we'll need high-level pricing to decide.

Procurement will coordinate scheduling; happy to meet for 30 minutes after we get the initial spreadsheet.

Jordan
Head of Integrations | Acme Health
jordan@acmehealth.com
